question: When Elena Mistrello, an Italian comic book author and EU citizen, landed at the airport in France on 21 November 2025, she was refused entry into the country, despite having been invited to the BD Colomiers comics festival to introduce her award-winning book Syndrome Italie.

She was informed by the border police that she was a ‘serious threat to public policy’ and discovered that she was subject to an entry ban, without having been previously informed of such a decision or its legal basis.

Directive 2004/38/EC grants EU citizens the right to enter another Member State (Articles 4 and 5), and restrictions on grounds of public policy must be based on the personal conduct of the person concerned, constitute a sufficiently serious threat and comply with the principles of necessity and proportionality, as well as with procedural safeguards, such as notification of the decision and access to judicial review (Articles 27, 28 and 30 to 32).

How does the Commission intend to ensure that France and the other Member States strictly apply those requirements, particularly when the grounds relied on relate to political, artistic or cultural expression?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.2.2026) Member States may restrict the freedom of movement of EU citizens on grounds of public policy or public security, provided that they respect the substantive and procedural safeguards set out in the Free Movement Directive 2004/38/EC1.

In particular, restrictive measures may be taken only on a case-by-case basis where the personal conduct of an individual represents a genuine, present and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of the society of the host Member State. Decisions must be proportionate and based on an individual assessment.

The persons concerned must be informed, precisely and in full, of the grounds of the decision, unless this is contrary to the interests of State security, and must have access to judicial and, where appropriate, administrative redress procedures.

In individual cases, national courts are competent to establish whether a misapplication of EU law, including a violation of fundamental rights, has taken place and to award compensation to persons who suffered damages. The Commission works closely with Member States to monitor and promote the correct application of EU free movement law.
The Commission guidance on free movement2 covers, among others, restrictions on grounds of public policy and public security and the relative safeguards.
1 Directive 2004/38/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the right of citizens

of the Union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the Member States, OJ L 158, 30.4.2004, pp. 77–123. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:C_202301392.
